title: Look-Fors That Look for Learning
tagline: Leaders sort walkthrough notes, practice on three classroom vignettes, and rebuild their technology observation tool so it captures evidence of learning instead of counting devices.
groupSize: Teams of 3–5; ideally a campus leadership team with its coach
overview: Many walkthrough forms still ask "Are students using technology?" and a yes feels like success. The updated ELEs say plainly that technology use by itself is not evidence of learning. In this session, leaders sort real-sounding walkthrough notes into evidence of learning versus evidence of device use, calibrate on three classroom vignettes (including one with generative AI), and revise a starter observation rubric so it asks what students are thinking, verifying, and deciding. They leave with a tool they can pilot in next week's walkthroughs.
objectives: Participants will distinguish walkthrough observations that show evidence of learning from those that show only device or tool use.
Participants will calibrate their ratings on three classroom vignettes and explain the evidence behind each rating.
Participants will revise an observation rubric so its criteria name student thinking, verification of information and AI output, and access, and pilot one criterion within a week.

print: Handout A: Walkthrough Notes Sort (1 mat and 1 set of strips per team)
Handout B: Three Classroom Vignettes (1 per person)
Handout C: Starter Look-For Rubric (1 per person, plus 1 enlarged per team for revision)
Your campus's current walkthrough form (1 per team), highlighters in two colors
digital: Optional: two or three short classroom video clips your district has permission to use, as a substitute for or addition to Handout B
Optional: a digital form version of the revised rubric for piloting on a phone or tablet during walkthroughs

prep: Print and cut Handout A into strips; one envelope per team.
Collect your campus's current technology walkthrough form, or any district observation tool, and remove any teacher names from sample completed forms.
If you use video, preview clips for student privacy and permissions. Never use video of students without the district's media release process.
Decide which days next week leaders will pilot the revised rubric so the Transfer step ends with a real date.

steps.title: What does your form count?
steps.body: Teams look at their current walkthrough form and highlight in one color every item that could be checked **just by seeing a device or app** ("Students are using technology," "Teacher uses interactive display"). In the other color, highlight every item that requires **seeing student thinking**. Ask: **"Which color is winning?"**
steps.note: In most rooms, device-use items outnumber learning items. Don't shame the form; many were written when access itself was the goal. The goal has changed.

steps.title: Sort the notes
steps.body: Teams sort the 14 walkthrough note strips from Handout A into three columns: **Evidence of learning, Evidence of device use only, Needs more context.** For every "Needs more context" strip, write the one question you'd ask a student to find out. Check against the facilitator key and discuss any disagreements.
steps.note: The "Needs more context" column is where leaders learn the most. "Students are using an AI chatbot" tells you nothing until you ask a student what they're doing with its answer.

steps.title: The two-minute student conversation
steps.body: Model how to gather learning evidence during a short visit. Role-play with a volunteer playing a student from Vignette A. Ask three questions aloud: **"What are you working on and why?" "How do you know that's right?" "What did you change and what made you change it?"** Point out that none of these questions mentions the device.
steps.note: Leaders often observe from the back of the room. Evidence of learning usually requires kneeling beside a student and asking.

steps.title: Calibrate on three vignettes
steps.body: Each person reads the three vignettes on Handout B and scores each using the Starter Look-For Rubric (Handout C), writing the **specific evidence** from the vignette beside each score. Teams then compare scores criterion by criterion. Where scores differ by more than one level, the team rereads the vignette and agrees on what evidence would settle it.
steps.note: Vignette C (the tablet reading station) is designed to score high on device use and low on learning evidence. Vignette B (the paper-only lesson) has no devices at all and scores well on several criteria. Both are intentional.

steps.title: Rebuild the rubric
steps.body: Using the enlarged Handout C, teams revise the starter rubric for their campus. They may reword, cut, or add criteria, but each criterion must pass two tests: **(1) It can be scored only by seeing or hearing student work or talk. (2) It fits a lesson with no devices as well as one with many.** Teams add one research-based practice their campus already values (for example, timely feedback, retrieval practice, or students explaining their reasoning) as a criterion or a descriptor.
steps.note: Keep the tool short. Four or five criteria that leaders actually use are better than twelve they skim. Remind teams that a walkthrough tool supports coaching conversations; it should not become a compliance checklist.

steps.title: Stress test with a colleague's eye
steps.body: Teams swap rubrics and score Vignette A again with the other team's version. Ask: **"Did this rubric capture what mattered in the vignette? What would a teacher learn from receiving this feedback?"** Each team takes back one suggestion.
steps.note: Listen for rubrics that still reward AI use as a good in itself. The question is whether students questioned and verified the AI output, and whether the AI made their thinking more visible or did the thinking for them.

steps.title: Pilot plan
steps.body: Each team chooses **one criterion** to pilot in walkthroughs next week, names who will visit which classrooms, and agrees on how they'll share the evidence with teachers as a coaching conversation. Write the pilot plan on the back of Handout C.
steps.note: Suggest leaders tell teachers in advance what the pilot criterion is. Transparency makes it a shared learning goal rather than a surprise evaluation.

unplugged: The sort, vignettes, and rubric revision all run on paper, and the two-minute student conversation is a live role-play. Leaders can pilot the revised rubric on a clipboard. Nothing in the session requires a device.
digital: Replace or supplement the written vignettes with two or three short classroom videos your district has permission to use, and calibrate by having everyone submit scores to a simple form so the spread is visible immediately. After the session, build the revised rubric as a mobile form so walkthrough evidence can be aggregated by criterion across the campus and reviewed with the coach.
whyTech: Collecting calibration scores digitally shows the spread of ratings in seconds, which makes disagreements visible and discussable. A digital walkthrough form lets leaders see patterns across many visits, such as how often students verify AI output, that paper forms scatter across clipboards.

adaptations.label: Higher Ed
adaptations.text: Use the protocol for peer observation of teaching, replacing the vignettes with a lecture with polling, a lab, and a seminar. Emphasize that observation is formative and voluntary where faculty governance requires it.

adaptations.label: Elementary campuses
adaptations.text: Rewrite Vignette C as a K–2 center rotation and add a criterion about students explaining their thinking orally, since young students' evidence is often spoken rather than written.

adaptations.label: Coaches only
adaptations.text: Use the revised rubric as a self-assessment tool that teachers choose to use with their coach, not an observation form.

lookFors: Teams correctly place at least 11 of 14 strips and write a specific student question for each "Needs more context" strip.
Calibration discussions cite specific evidence from the vignettes rather than general impressions.
Every criterion in the revised rubric can be scored in a lesson with no devices, and at least one criterion addresses verification of information or AI output.
Each team leaves with a named criterion, dates, and a plan for sharing evidence with teachers.
reflection: In what ways am I supporting and evaluating effective use of educational technology across our school? (Leader ELE 2.0)
What does our current walkthrough tool reward, and what message does that send to teachers?
How would I evaluate whether an AI-enhanced lesson improved learning rather than just speeding up task completion? (AI ELE 3.0)
What will I do differently during my next classroom visit?
transfer: Next week, pilot one criterion from your revised rubric in at least five classrooms, using the two-minute student conversation in each. Share what you saw with the teachers as questions, not scores, and bring the patterns to your next leadership meeting.

handouts.title: Walkthrough Notes Sort
handouts.instructions: Each strip is a note a leader wrote during a five-minute visit. Sort it. For any "Needs more context" strip, write the question you'd ask a student.

items.text: All students logged in and working on the platform within two minutes.
items.why: Efficient routines matter, but logging in says nothing about learning.

items.text: A student explained why she rejected two of the AI chatbot's three suggested research questions: "One wasn't testable and one we already know the answer to."
items.why: The student evaluates AI output with a clear criterion.

items.text: Students are using an AI chatbot during writing time.
items.why: Ask: "What did you ask it, and what did you do with what it said?"

items.text: Teacher used the interactive display for the entire lesson.
items.why: Describes the teacher's tool, not student thinking.

items.text: Two students disagreed about a source's reliability and each pointed to who published it and whether other sources confirmed it.
items.why: Lateral reading and evidence-based reasoning are visible in student talk.

items.text: 100% of students completed the online quiz; class average 84%.
items.why: Ask: "What was the quiz measuring, and what will the teacher do with the results?"

items.text: A student's revision history showed she rewrote her claim after peer feedback and noted why.
items.why: Revision with a reason is strong evidence; the tool made it visible.

items.text: Students watching a video with headphones.
items.why: Ask: "What are you listening for, and what will you do with it?"

items.text: Students made slideshows about the water cycle with animations and sound effects.
items.why: Ask a student to explain one step of the cycle without the slides. Product polish isn't understanding.

items.text: Students used a digital annotation tool to mark claims and evidence; one flagged a statistic with no source.
Every student had a device open.
items.why: Presence of devices is not evidence of anything.

items.text: In a no-device lesson, small groups sorted cards and justified each placement to the teacher.
Students used an AI-generated study guide.
items.why: Ask: "Did you check anything in it? Was anything wrong?"

items.text: A student using speech-to-text dictated his lab conclusion and then edited it for accuracy.
items.why: Assistive technology gives access, and the editing shows his thinking.

handouts.title: Three Classroom Vignettes
handouts.instructions: These classrooms are fictional. Score each with the Starter Look-For Rubric and write the evidence beside each score.
paragraphs: **Vignette A · 8th Grade Science, Ms. Okada.** Students are designing an investigation on what affects how fast ice melts. Ms. Okada projects a district-approved AI chatbot and asks it for ten investigation questions. She hands each team a printout of the list. Teams must choose one, reject at least two with a reason, and check whether their chosen question is testable with the materials available.

When you visit, one team is arguing about whether "Does salt melt ice faster than sugar?" is fair because the amounts aren't specified. Another student says, "The AI said colored ice melts faster in sunlight, but it didn't say why, so we're testing it." On the board: "Reject list: what we didn't pick and why." A student who recently arrived from Brazil is working with a partner, using a bilingual glossary card.

**Vignette B · 4th Grade Reading, Mr. Hollis.** No devices are in use. Students are in pairs with two short printed articles about whether the town should build a skate park, one from the town newspaper and one from a skate shop's flyer. Each pair fills in a T-chart: "What does it claim? Who made it? What do they want?"

When you ask a student which article she trusts more, she says, "The newspaper, because the flyer is trying to sell skateboards, so of course they want the park." Her partner adds, "But the newspaper only talked to two people." Mr. Hollis circulates, asking "How do you know?" After ten minutes, pairs share one sentence each with the class.

**Vignette C · 6th Grade Math, Ms. Grant.** Every student has a tablet. Students work through an adaptive practice program on fractions that awards badges and points. The dashboard on Ms. Grant's screen shows green, yellow, and red dots for each student. Ms. Grant is at her desk updating the grade book.

When you ask a student what he's learning, he says, "Fractions. I'm on level 12." When you ask him to explain why 3/4 is bigger than 2/3, he says, "I don't know, I just click until it's right, and then it gives me the next one." Two students in the back have headphones in and are on the same screen they were on when you arrived.

handouts.title: Starter Look-For Rubric
handouts.instructions: A starting point for revision, not a finished tool. Each criterion should be scorable only by seeing or hearing student work or talk, with or without devices.

criteria.name: Purpose of the task
descriptors: Students can't say what they're learning, only what they're doing or which tool they're using.
Some students can name the learning goal when asked.
Most students can name the learning goal and how the task helps them reach it.
Students explain the goal and why they chose a tool, format, or approach (including no tool) to reach it.

criteria.name: Student thinking made visible
descriptors: Work shows answers only; no reasoning is visible or audible.
Some reasoning is visible, mostly prompted by the teacher.
Students explain or show reasoning in talk, writing, annotation, or revision.
Students revise their thinking and can say what changed it.

criteria.name: Verification of information and AI output
descriptors: Information or AI output is accepted as given.
Students check some information when prompted.
Students question sources or AI output and check claims against other sources.
Students name how they verified, what they rejected or corrected, and why.

criteria.name: Ownership and choice
descriptors: All students follow the same steps with no decisions to make.
Students make minor choices (order, format).
Students make meaningful decisions about approach, sources, or product.
Students set goals, choose approaches, and reflect on whether their choices worked.

criteria.name: Access and inclusion
descriptors: Some students cannot participate fully (language, accessibility, device, or connection barriers are visible).
Supports exist but not all students who need them are using them.
Supports (language, accessibility, alternatives) are in use and students participate fully.
Students use supports independently and the task offers more than one way to show learning.
